title: hung-hems
questionDisplay: A clean folded hem: knit the hem, make a turning row, rehang the stitches, and knit it in place.
keyInsight: A hung hem succeeds when the fold line is intentional (turning row) and the rehang/join is even — most “problem hems” come from bulk, mismatch, or uneven rehanging, not from the basic technique.
quickCheckText: If the fold line looks crisp and the rehang row sits flat with even stitch spacing, your hem will hang cleanly and wear well.
body:
A hung hem is a folded hem that you knit in two layers, then join by rehanging the hem stitches onto the needles and knitting them together. It creates a tidy finish with a little built-in weight, which helps the edge hang nicely.

When a hung hem is a good choice

  • You want a clean, polished edge without ribbing.
  • You want a hem that adds a little structure and weight.
  • You’re finishing a sweater hem, sleeve hem, or another straight edge.

What makes it work

  • The turning row creates the fold line (this controls how crisp or decorative the fold looks).
  • The rehang + join row locks the fold in place and keeps the edge neat.
  • Small tension changes inside the hem can help it sit flatter and hang better.

Common variations

  • Classic turning row: a simple fold line for a plain hem.
  • Decorative turning row: eyelets, a garter-style row, or another effect for detail at the fold.
  • Tension tweak: slightly looser or tighter hem sections to control rolling and bulk.

If your hem isn’t behaving

  • Hem flips out: try a slightly deeper hem, or adjust the turning-row/tension so it wants to fold inward.
  • Hem feels bulky: reduce hem depth, use a smoother turning row, or choose a yarn that folds cleanly.
  • Hem edge looks wavy: check that the rehang count matches the needle spacing and the stitches are seated evenly.
shortAnswer: A hung hem is a clean, folded hem that’s formed by knitting a hem section, creating a turning row, then rehanging the live stitches to knit the hem in place. It’s a great choice when you want a neat edge with a little weight and a polished look. Use it on sweater hems, sleeves, and other edges where you want the fabric to hang nicely without adding ribbing.
outcomeLine: A hung hem is a reliable finish you can adapt endlessly — once you understand the fold, the tension, and the rehang, it becomes one of the most useful techniques in machine knitting.
steps: Knit the hem depth you want (often ¾"–1½").
Knit a turning row to create the fold line.
Knit the same depth again (or knit to your garment measurement).
Rehang the cast-on/live hem stitches onto the needles.
Knit one row to join the hem, then continue your garment.
If the hem rolls or flips, adjust hem tension or turning-row choice.
